props.title: Flesh

sections.content: Paul Morrissey's **Flesh** (1968) revolutionized independent cinema with its raw portrayal of street hustling in New York City. Produced by Andy Warhol, the film stars Joe Dallesandro in a breakthrough performance that made him an underground icon. The documentary-style approach and unflinching examination of sex work, drug use, and queer life challenged censorship standards and influenced decades of indie filmmakers. Like **Midnight Cowboy** (1969) and **My Own Private Idaho** (1991), Flesh explores male prostitution but with Warhol's signature blend of voyeurism and detachment.

sections.content: The Factory scene that produced Flesh marked a crucial transition in American independent film. While Warhol's earlier experimental works like **Chelsea Girls** (1966) were largely non-narrative, Morrissey brought a stronger storytelling focus while maintaining the raw authenticity. The film's influence can be seen in later works like **Cruising** (1980) and **Looking for Langston** (1989), which similarly explored underground queer spaces with documentary elements.

Flesh's technical approach - long takes, natural lighting, improvised dialogue - established a new aesthetic for depicting marginalized communities. Later films like **Paris is Burning** (1990) and **Kids** (1995) adopted similar strategies to capture urban subcultures. The film's frank sexuality pushed boundaries that even contemporary queer cinema rarely approaches. SUBHEAD: Impact on New Queer Cinema

sections.content: Flesh laid groundwork for the New Queer Cinema movement of the 1990s. Directors like Gus Van Sant and Todd Haynes have acknowledged its influence on films like **Poison** (1991) and **Swoon** (1992). The film's matter-of-fact treatment of sexuality and gender fluidity was decades ahead of its time, predating similar themes in **Hedwig and the Angry Inch** (2001) and **Shortbus** (2006).
